title: Clinical and prescription abbreviations
note: Many dosing abbreviations come from Latin: bid (bis in die, twice a day), prn (pro re nata, as needed), po (per os, by mouth). The Joint Commission's Do Not Use list bans U, IU, QD, QOD, trailing zeros, missing leading zeros, and MS, MSO4 and MgSO4 in medication documentation; write the full term instead.

read.title: Why some abbreviations are banned
text: Abbreviations save time, but a misread abbreviation can deliver the wrong drug, the wrong dose or the wrong schedule. The Joint Commission, which accredits hospitals in the United States, keeps a short Do Not Use list that applies to all orders, preprinted forms and medication-related documentation, whether handwritten or electronic.

Each item is on the list because it is easily misread. A handwritten U for unit can look like a 0 or a 4, so 4U can be read as 40; the word unit is written out instead. IU can be read as IV. QD (daily) and QOD (every other day) are easily confused with each other, so daily and every other day are spelled out. MS and its variants can mean either morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate, two very different drugs.

Two rules concern decimal points. A trailing zero, as in 5.0 mg, is not used in medication orders because a missed decimal turns it into 50 mg. A leading zero is always required before a decimal, as in 0.5 mg, because .5 mg can be read as 5 mg.
Standard abbreviations such as bid, tid, prn, PO and NPO remain in common use, and many organizations also keep their own lists of approved abbreviations.
